CPM Pedagogical Theory

Strategies

📓 Using Gemini Notebook to Build a Course

This tab doesn't generate anything itself — it explains a technique. Upload your own material (a textbook chapter, a PDF, past resources, research) into a Gemini Notebook, then work through these prompts in order to turn it into a fully-staged course.

Why staged prompting, not one giant prompt

Asking an AI for "a whole course" in one shot tends to produce something shallow — it has to spread its attention across eight different jobs at once. Working in stages, and explicitly pausing between each one, keeps every step grounded in what actually came before it, and keeps the output dense rather than thin. This is the exact same principle behind two things already built into this tool: Lesson Builder's Gemini Notebook mode generates its source document and its slide prompt as separate, sequential pieces rather than one pass, and Unit Planner's Gemini Notebook add-on deliberately stops and asks before it writes the follow-up knowledge document. The sequence below is that same idea, taken all the way through a full course.

The 8-Step Sequence

Work through these in order, inside the same Gemini Notebook chat. Replace [TOPIC], [AUDIENCE], and [X] each time — Gemini will have already told you the module/lesson numbers from Step 1's output.

Step 1 — Create the Course Blueprint

Using the sources in this notebook, create a complete course on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. Build a logical beginner-to-advanced curriculum with 6–10 modules, learning objectives, lessons and practical outcomes for each module.

Run this first, once, before anything else — everything downstream refers back to the module/lesson structure it produces.

Step 2 — Build Each Module

Expand Module [X] into a complete learning module. Include the module objective, key concepts, 3–5 lessons, examples, exercises and expected outcomes. Base everything on the notebook sources.

Repeat once per module, one at a time — not all at once — so each one gets full attention.

Step 3 — Create the Lessons

Turn Lesson [X] into a detailed lesson. Include what students need to know, a clear explanation, step-by-step teaching points, examples, common mistakes and an actionable exercise.

Repeat per lesson within the module you're working on.

Step 4 — Create Teaching Scripts

Write a conversational teaching script for Lesson [X] that I can use for a video or live class. Start with a strong hook, explain each concept simply, use examples and finish with an action step.

Optional — only worth doing for lessons you're actually recording or presenting live.

Step 5 — Create Study Materials

Create supporting materials for Module [X]. Include a concise summary, key takeaways, important terminology, cheat sheet, reflection questions and practical exercises students can use after the lesson.

One per module, once that module's lessons are done.

Step 6 — Create Quizzes

Create a 10-question quiz for Module [X] based only on the notebook sources. Mix multiple-choice, true/false and scenario-based questions. Include the correct answers and short explanations.

"Based only on the notebook sources" matters — it's what stops Gemini inventing facts that aren't actually in your material.

Step 7 — Create Assignments

Create a practical assignment for Module [X] that requires students to apply what they learned. Include the objective, instructions, deliverables, assessment criteria and an example of a strong submission.

One per module — this is the "prove you can actually use it" check, not just the recall check the quiz already covers.

Step 8 — Create the Final Project

Design a final project that combines everything taught throughout the course. Give students a realistic outcome to produce, step-by-step instructions, deliverables, grading criteria and a checklist for successful completion.

Last step, once — after every module is built, not before.

📚 Credits & Sources

This tool draws on published pedagogical research and official curriculum materials. It paraphrases and references these works to guide AI-generated content — it does not reproduce their text.

Curriculum & Framework Sources

  • Common Practice Model (CPM) — New Zealand Ministry of Education, Te Mahau.
  • Te Mātaiaho — the New Zealand Curriculum refresh, Ministry of Education. Science and Social Sciences Years 0–10 content was finalised and published on Tāhūrangi on 12 August 2026, and the Year Planner is drawn from those final documents. Since v2.6 the Year Planner's Science, English, Maths, PE & Health and The Arts libraries are generated from the same curriculum data as the Unit Planner picker. Other learning areas (Maths, English, PE & Health, etc.) are still drawn from Te Mātaiaho draft materials pending their final release.
  • Inbuilt curriculum content (Unit Planner) — English, Maths, Science, Social Sciences, The Arts and Health & PE, Years 7–10, taken from the Ministry's teaching sequences as reproduced in the WHS Curriculum 7–10 reference pages (English and Maths 2025; Science August 2026; Social Sciences, The Arts and Health & PE September 2026). Every fill-in names its source document.
  • Student AI use options — the AI levels, AI use statement and teacher check questions are from the WHS Brain Before AI site, and the traffic-light status from the WHS AI Traffic Light for NCEA internal assessments.
  • Make a Explore Board — the ring layout is after the Multimedia Text Set template by Genevieve Pacada, remixed by Jennifer Wolfe. HyperDocs by Lisa Highfill.
  • Make a Quiz — file layouts follow the published import templates of Kahoot, Blooket, Gimkit, Quizizz and Quizlet. These are independent products; the WHS Quiz Maker is not connected to or endorsed by them.
  • NCEA Achievement Standards — New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA). This tool never invents or guesses standard numbers/titles; teachers supply these directly.

Teaching Strategy Sources (Strategy suggestions in Lesson Builder & Unit Planner)

  • Ginnis, P. — The Teacher's Toolkit. Source for strategies including Concept Frame, Quick on the Draw, The Value Continuum, and others.
  • Whitehead, D. — the Top Tools series. Source for strategies including Fiction Meaning Grid, Mental Time Travel (MTW), CREATE Metaphor Construction, and others.
  • Cubitt, C., Irvine, R., & Dow, S. — Top Tools for Social Sciences Teachers. Source for graphic organiser strategies including Fishbone Diagram, Flow Chart, T-Chart/SEEC Analysis, I-Chart, and Mind Mapping.

Design & Branding

  • Waiheke High School subject colour palette, logo, and WHS Official Templates — used with permission for internal school use.

Evidence for AI as a Learning Support

  • Fischer, M., Rau, H. A., & Rilke, R. M. (2025) — "AI Tutoring Enhances Student Learning Without Crowding Out Reading Effort", IZA Discussion Paper No. 18338. A randomised trial found AI tutor access raised test performance without reducing how much students actually read the source material — evidence that, used well, AI adds to student effort rather than replacing it.
  • Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., & Ponti, G. (2025) — "AI Tutoring Outperforms In-Class Active Learning", Scientific Reports 15, 17458. This Harvard-led randomised trial found students learned significantly more, in less time, with a well-designed AI tutor than in an active-learning classroom — itself already considered best practice, not a passive lecture — while also reporting higher engagement and motivation.

🧘 A Moment for You

Take a minute before you get back to it.

Breathe In

4 secs in · hold · 4 secs out

📖 Eat Your Ice Cream: Six Simple Rules for a Long & Healthy Life

Dr. Ezekiel J. Emanuel — oncologist, bioethicist, and health policy expert

The book is a grounded, evidence-based antidote to what the author calls the "wellness industrial complex" — the billion-dollar industry of biohacks, rigid diets, unproven longevity fads, and obsessive tracking. Emanuel's core argument: health should be an invisible, effortless background habit, not a stressful full-time job, and a long life is only valuable if it's joyful and meaningful.

Key Themes & Takeaways

  • Wellness is a means, not the end. Living longer isn't a competition — the goal of health is simply to give you the vitality to enjoy your life, foster relationships, and engage with your community.
  • The metaphor behind the title. "Eat your ice cream" is a call for balance over extreme deprivation. Joy, social connection, and mental satisfaction play a massive role in longevity — sometimes even more than hyper-strict physical habits.
  • 6 evidence-based pillars, distilled from decades of medical research:
    1. Nutrition — real food, less processed sugar, shared meals
    2. Exercise — consistency through enjoyable movement over extreme workouts
    3. Sleep — regular rest without obsessive gadget tracking
    4. Alcohol — sensible limits rather than panic
    5. Mental Acuity — lifelong curiosity and learning
    6. Social Connection — one of the strongest indicators of long-term health

"Life is not a competition to live the longest, and wellness should not be a full-time job."

A practical, common-sense roadmap to living well — without letting the pursuit of perfect health consume your happiness.

🏫 Turning the AI's output into a Doc

The AI will return a block of HTML code. Here's the quickest way to turn it into a real, formatted Google Doc.

Quickest option: if your AI's response shows a download button or icon near the code block, click that first — it'll save the HTML file directly, skipping steps 1 and 2 below (you'll still need step 3 to open it). Not every AI shows this, so if you don't see one, just follow all the steps manually instead:
  1. 1 Copy only the code from the AI's reply — everything between the ```html and the closing ```, not the backticks themselves.
  2. 2 Paste it into a plain text editor — Notepad (Windows) or TextEdit (Mac, first switch to Format → Make Plain Text) — and save it as UnitPlan.html.
  3. 3 Double-click that file to open it in your web browser — it'll render as a formatted page with real tables and colours.
  4. 4 Select everything and copy it: Ctrl+A then Ctrl+C (Mac: Cmd+A then Cmd+C).
  5. 5 Open a new Google Doc and set it to Landscape first — File → Page setup → Orientation → Landscape — since this template is designed for a wide layout.
  6. 6 Paste into the doc: Ctrl+V (Mac: Cmd+V). Tables, shading, and borders should come through — you may just need to nudge column widths afterwards.
